blocks.text: 12.5.6 CI/CD With GitHub Actions

Everything is now in place to deploy GridCap's service: an image (lesson 12.5.1), the Batch and Step Functions design (lesson 12.5.2), the store and index (lesson 12.5.3), a moto test suite (lesson 12.5.4), and the Terraform (lesson 12.5.5). Done by hand, a release is a dozen commands typed in the right order by whoever has the AWS keys, and the day someone skips the tests or applies from a stale branch, the plan of record runs on code nobody reviewed. **CI/CD** (continuous integration and delivery) moves those commands into a file in the repository that a service runs on every change: the tests on every pull request, and the build and deploy on every merge to `main`. This lesson reads GridCap's workflow for **GitHub Actions**, GitHub's CI service, and checks it with a program. (GridCap is fictional; no number in it is real.)

**This lesson is read-along for its workflow.** The course does not run GitHub Actions: the file lives at `deploy/github-workflows/ci.yml`, not under `.github/workflows/`, so no service runs it. `workflow_review.py` parses it and reasons about it, and its output is printed. No model is built or changed here.
A Workflow Is Jobs, a Job Is Steps, and needs Orders the Jobs

A **workflow** is a YAML file. `on` names the events that start it; `jobs` holds the **jobs**, each run on a fresh machine (a **runner**) as a list of **steps**: a shell command (`run`) or a reusable **action** (`uses`). Jobs run in parallel unless one **needs** another. The head of GridCap's workflow:

name: ci

on:
  pull_request:
  push:
    branches: [main]

permissions:
  contents: read

It starts on every pull request, and on every push to `main` (a merge). Its three jobs are `test`, `image` (needs `test`) and `deploy` (needs `test` and `image`), and the last two carry `if: github.event_name == 'push'`. GitHub's workflow syntax reference states the rule that decides what runs: if a job's `if` is false it is skipped, and if a job it needs fails or is skipped, it is skipped too, all the way down the chain, unless its `if` uses a function such as `always()`. `workflow_review.py` applies that rule to the file for each event:

pull_request  {'test': 'runs', 'image': 'skipped', 'deploy': 'skipped'}
push          {'test': 'runs', 'image': 'runs', 'deploy': 'runs'}

A pull request runs only the tests. A merge runs all three, in order, and a failing test stops the build and the deploy, because they need it. (The program reads only this file's simple `if`s; it is a model of the rule, not of GitHub's expression language.)
One trap when a program reads a workflow. PyYAML follows YAML 1.1, in which a bare `on` is a boolean, so the key comes back as `True`:
top-level keys: ['name', True, 'permissions', 'env', 'jobs']
GitHub reads the file its own way, so the workflow is fine; a script that looks up `flow["on"]` gets a `KeyError`. Quote it (`"on":`) or look up `True` when you parse workflows yourself.
Tests Run on Every Change, Against moto, With No Credentials
The `test` job is the course's own habit, moved to a server:

test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-24.04
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@0000000000000000000000000000000000000000  # v5
      - uses: actions/setup-python@0000000000000000000000000000000000000000  # v6
        with:
          python-version: "3.14"
      - run: pip install -r requirements.txt
      - run: python -m pytest       # moto only: this job has no AWS credentials at all

The suite of lesson 12.5.4 needs no AWS, so this job is given none: it has no role and the workflow references no secrets. A test that escaped moto would fail with `NoCredentialsError` (lesson 12.5.4's first output), not reach an account. The job pins the runner image (`ubuntu-24.04`) and the Python version, for the reason lesson 12.5.1 pinned the solver: a result that changes when the machine changes is not a test.
CI Gets AWS Access From OIDC, Never From Stored Keys

The `image` and `deploy` jobs must act in AWS. The old way stores an access key as a repository secret; it never expires, and anyone who can change a workflow can print it. GitHub's documentation describes the replacement, **OpenID Connect (OIDC)**: the job asks GitHub for a short-lived signed token that says which repository, branch and environment it runs for, and AWS exchanges it for temporary credentials of a role whose trust policy accepts exactly those claims (the audience `sts.amazonaws.com`, and a subject naming the repository). Nothing long-lived exists to steal. In the workflow it takes two things:

permissions:
      contents: read
      id-token: write

- uses: aws-actions/configure-aws-credentials@0000000000000000000000000000000000000000  # v5
        with:
          role-to-assume: arn:aws:iam::123456789012:role/gridcap-ci-push
          aws-region: us-east-1

`id-token: write` lets the job request the token; `configure-aws-credentials` trades it for the role's credentials. Each job assumes its own role: `gridcap-ci-push` may push images to the registry, `gridcap-ci-deploy` may apply Terraform. The program confirms no secret is referenced anywhere:
secrets referenced: []
Pin Every Action to a Commit and Give the Token Least Privilege

An action is someone else's code running with your job's permissions. A tag such as `@v5` can be moved by whoever controls the action's repository, so the next run can execute different code. GitHub's security-hardening guide recommends pinning each action to a full-length commit SHA, which cannot move, with the version in a comment for people. The SHAs in this file are all zeros: placeholders, because the course cannot look up and verify each release's commit. A real workflow replaces each with the commit of the release its comment names.

The same guide says to give the workflow's `GITHUB_TOKEN` (the credential every job gets for GitHub itself) the least access it needs. The workflow sets `contents: read` at the top, and only the two jobs that talk to AWS add `id-token: write`. The program prints each job's needs, permissions, pins and environment:

test    needs -                 permissions {'contents': 'read'}, every action SHA-pinned: True, environment: -
image   needs ['test']          permissions {'contents': 'read', 'id-token': 'write'}, every action SHA-pinned: True, environment: -
deploy  needs ['test', 'image'] permissions {'contents': 'read', 'id-token': 'write'}, every action SHA-pinned: True, environment: production

The workflow syntax reference says a `permissions` block sets every scope it does not name to `none`, and that the job's block is applied after the workflow's. So `image` and `deploy` repeat `contents: read`, which checking out the code needs; without it they would have `id-token` alone.
<!-- practice 1 -->
Deploy Builds One Image per Commit, Then Plans, Checks and Applies Behind an Environment
The `image` job tags each image with the commit that built it, `${{ github.sha }}`, and pushes it to the immutable repository of lesson 12.5.5:

- run: docker build -t "$REGISTRY/gridcap-solver:${{ github.sha }}" .
      - run: docker push "$REGISTRY/gridcap-solver:${{ github.sha }}"

Every image is then traceable to a commit, and every run's container to its image. A planner's question "which code solved this?" has an answer: the job definition names the tag, and the tag is the commit.
The `deploy` job runs lesson 12.5.5's loop, with its check between plan and apply:

- run: terraform -chdir=deploy/terraform show -json tfplan > plan.json
      - run: python plan_guard.py plan.json      # the plan gate: refuses a plan that destroys history
      - run: terraform -chdir=deploy/terraform apply -input=false tfplan

`plan_guard.py` is the service repository's copy of lesson 12.5.5's rule, exiting non-zero on a blocked plan. A non-zero exit fails the step, the job stops, and `apply` never runs. The plan is made with the new image's tag as `-var "image=..."`, so the job definition's revision points at exactly the image this run built.

The job also names an **environment**, `production`. In GitHub, an environment can carry protection rules, such as required reviewers (up to six; one approval is enough); the workflow syntax reference says every protection rule must pass before a job that references the environment is sent to a runner. So a merge to `main` runs the tests and builds the image by itself, and the apply waits for a person to approve it.
<!-- practice 2 -->
Summary

items: **A workflow is jobs, a job is steps, and `needs` orders the jobs.** A job whose need failed or was skipped is skipped; pull requests run the tests only. PyYAML reads `on` as `True`.
**Tests run on every change, against moto, with no credentials.**
**CI gets AWS access from OIDC, never from stored keys.** `id-token: write` and a role per job.
**Pin every action to a commit and give the token least privilege.** A `permissions` block sets every scope it does not name to `none`.
**Deploy builds one image per commit, then plans, checks and applies behind an environment.**

blocks.text: Reference

rows: the events that start the workflow
run after `a` and `b` succeed; skipped if either fails or is skipped
skip the job when false; `always()` runs it whatever its needs did
protection rules (reviewers) pass before the job runs
an action pinned to a commit

blocks.text: **Further reading:** OR-Tools, [Installing OR-Tools for Python](https://developers.google.com/optimization/install/python) (what CI's `pip install` fetches); GitHub, [Workflow syntax for GitHub Actions](https://docs.github.com/en/actions/writing-workflows/workflow-syntax-for-github-actions) (`on`, `needs` and skipped jobs, `if`, `permissions`, `environment`), [Security hardening for GitHub Actions](https://docs.github.com/en/actions/security-for-github-actions/security-guides/security-hardening-for-github-actions) (SHA pinning, least-privilege `GITHUB_TOKEN`, OIDC over stored secrets), [Configuring OpenID Connect in Amazon Web Services](https://docs.github.com/en/actions/deployment/security-hardening-your-deployments/configuring-openid-connect-in-amazon-web-services) (`id-token: write`, `role-to-assume`, the trust policy's `aud` and `sub`) and [Managing environments for deployment](https://docs.github.com/en/actions/managing-workflow-runs-and-deployments/managing-deployments/managing-environments-for-deployment) (required reviewers); Terraform, [JSON output format](https://developer.hashicorp.com/terraform/internals/json-format).
Challenges

items: Add a `plan` job that runs on pull requests and prints the plan for reviewers, without being able to apply it. Which role does it assume, and what may that role do?
A workflow step runs `pip install -r requirements.txt`. What could still differ between two runs a month apart, and what would make them identical?
Make the `deploy` job also run when `image` was skipped because the image for this commit already exists. Write the `if`, and say what you must check first.

blocks.text: Design Note: The Pipeline Is Part of the Model's Trust

Section 10 made the solve repeatable and section 12 made it testable. CI is where both are enforced: the determinism and golden tests of lessons 12.3.3 and 12.3.4 run on every change, no code reaches the Batch job definition without passing them, and every result in S3 names a snapshot, every run an image, every image a commit. When a regulator asks how a plan was produced, the chain from the plan of record to the commit is written down by the pipeline, not reconstructed from memory.
The Full Programs

Each snippet above is part of a complete program, and each program printed the output the lesson shows. Open one to read it whole, change it, and run it again: Run starts the program on your copy of the code, so the course's own files never change.

**workflow_review.py.** Parses the workflow, works out which jobs run for each event, and prints each job's needs, permissions, pins and environment (all sections). *Try:* Replace one SHA in `ci.yml` with `v5`. Predict which job's line changes.
